answer: Each call at parameter mf makes s calls at parameter f, each on a stream of volume V/W, so the cost per unit of volume C satisfies C(mf) <= (s/W) C(f) + O(1). Unrolling this over log_m f levels, the deepest term is (s/W)^(log_m f) = f^(log_m(s/W)), so the cost per unit of data is a power of f with exponent log_m(s/W). That exponent is strictly below one exactly when s/W < m, that is s < Wm. Here s is the total rank of the frame changes over the edges of the linear exchange network, W is its wire count and m = h^3 is the dimension of the label space. The strict inequality is obtained from nested subspace labels: for the bit network s_b = W_b m - (N - 2L_b), which is below W_b m because L_b/N = 100/539 is below 1/2. For the saving to be a power, any fixed tau < 1 with s/W < m^tau works, and the wiki takes tau = 1 - 2^(-50). The relative deficit is tiny: eta_b = 339/22587335000000, about 1.5e-11, and eta_c is about 3.7e-12, but any positive deficit gives a power saving.

citations.quote: a call at parameter $mf$ makes $s$ calls at parameter $f$ on streams of volume $V/W$ with $s<Wm$
The deepest term is $(s/W)^{\log_m f}=f^{\log_m(s/W)}$; for $s/W>1$ the geometric sum is a constant times it
So any fixed $\tau<1$ with $s/W<m^\tau$ gives $\mathcal C(f)=O(f^\tau)$
Source dimensions sum to $N$, sink dimensions to $Nm+N(m-1)+(W-2N)m=Wm-N$.
A wire enters and leaves each gate with that gate's label, so its signed changes telescope to sink minus source dimension, summing to $Wm-2N$ over all wires.

key_idea.statement: Each level of the recursion multiplies the cost per unit of volume by s/W, while the parameter shrinks by a factor m, so when s/W is below m the cost per unit of data becomes a power of f with exponent log_m(s/W), which is below one.
key_idea.quote: The deepest term is $(s/W)^{\log_m f}=f^{\log_m(s/W)}$; for $s/W>1$ the geometric sum is a constant times it, and for $s/W\le1$ it is $O(\log f)$.

stuck.quote: An edge's frame change costs one call at parameter $f$ on that wire's stream per unit of rank
stuck.note: The claim that a frame change of rank r costs r smaller calls is asserted here and rests on the matrix shear page, which I did not open (budget). The dol page only says that an edge shears by the difference of endpoint matrices, costing one smaller call per unit of rank, without showing why.

stuck.quote: Every route must change frame in all $m$ dimensions, so if every wire climbed from dimension $0$ to $m$ the total would be exactly $Wm$, which, as shown below, saves nothing.
stuck.note: I could not see why a full climb of every wire gives exactly Wm, or why that means no saving, until the telescoping count on the dol page; the link from the sign-counting to the strict inequality took a second page.

stuck.quote: The later page [Pukezad](dol) makes this choice: it uses nested subspaces as frames, so that an edge costs one smaller call per unit of rank change.
stuck.note: The frames page says the interior frames should be chosen to make edges cheap, but does not say why nested subspaces achieve that. I got past it by reading the dol page, and I still could not see why nesting, rather than some other choice, is what makes each edge cost only its rank change.

reason: I am fairly confident in the main chain. The recurrence C(mf) <= (s/W) C(f) + O(1) on the rut page gives a power below one exactly when s < Wm, and the dol page supplies the count s_b = W_b m - (N - 2L_b) < W_b m with L_b/N = 100/539 < 1/2. The explicit exponent is checked against the numbers on the page. Gaps: I did not open the matrix shear page (kep) or the complex-network page (mot), so the rank-cost step and the complex-network formula are taken on the wiki's word. I also did not check the claim that nested subspaces are the right frames beyond the statement given.
